title: Andy Burnham says Cambridge row needs scrutiny, not abuse
content:
Cambridge chancellor Chris Smith has called for plagiarism allegations against academic Jason Arday to be examined properly, while warning against what he described as a racist online pile-on following the professor’s death.

## Andy Burnham and the Cambridge response

Speaking to the BBC, Smith said it was important that claims of plagiarism were rigorously investigated. At the same time, he said it was also right to refuse to join in what he called a racist feeding frenzy over a particular academic. He did not name Arday directly in the comments.

The remarks came after Arday was found dead at home in London on Friday, days after resigning from his post at Cambridge. Arday had stepped down on Aug. 5 after accusations that parts of his doctoral thesis had been plagiarised were widely reported in the media.

Arday was Cambridge’s youngest-ever black professor, a detail that has sharpened concern about how the case has been handled and discussed publicly. The university is now facing mounting questions over both its response to the allegations and its treatment of the academic.

## What happened to Jason Arday

According to the supplied report, Arday said he had reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure. After his death, his family blamed what they called a misinformation campaign.

The controversy has since spread beyond the university itself. By Monday morning, an online fundraising page for Arday’s family had raised more than £146,000. A petition demanding a public inquiry into the media coverage had gathered almost 32,400 signatures.

These reactions show how quickly a university disciplinary or reputational dispute can become a much wider public issue when race, media scrutiny and institutional trust overlap. In this case, the debate is not only about whether plagiarism allegations were properly examined, but also about how those allegations were framed and amplified.

## Why the case matters

The episode has put Cambridge under pressure to explain its handling of the affair, particularly because the accusations emerged publicly before Arday’s death and drew strong reactions from different sides. Smith’s comments suggest the university wants to separate two questions: whether plagiarism claims deserve investigation, and whether the public response crossed into racism.

The BBC also reported that James Cleverly said that quite possibly some of the scrutiny faced by Arday was motivated by racism. He added, according to the report, that the situation would never have come this far if people within the university establishment had acted differently.

Outside the university, Stand Up To Racism was due to hold a vigil in London’s Trafalgar Square on Monday evening and another in Cambridge.

The death has also prompted broader reflection on the treatment of black academics and the way allegations can escalate once they enter the public arena. For Cambridge, the immediate challenge is to address the questions over process and tone while the case continues to draw attention.

For now, the publicly available information points to two parallel developments: the allegations themselves remain a matter of scrutiny, and the fallout from the coverage has become a separate controversy in its own right.
